PRESUMPTION OF FRAUD OR UNDUE INFLUENCE — DONATIVE TRANSFERS TO A DISQUALIFIED PERSON — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET ON TRANSFERS TO A "DISQUALIFIED PERSON"
This Information Sheet describes California's statutory presumption, set out in Probate Code sections 21380 through 21392, that a donative transfer made by a will, trust, or other instrument to certain categories of "disqualified persons" — including the person who drafted the instrument, a fiduciary who transcribed it, and a care custodian of a dependent-adult transferor — is presumed to be the product of fraud or undue influence unless that presumption is rebutted or a statutory exception applies. It is prepared by Pat Morgan, whose relationship to Jordan Lee is: Drafter of the instrument. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference only. It does not itself determine that any specific instrument makes a donative transfer to a disqualified person, that any specific transfer is or is not presumed to be the product of fraud or undue influence, that any such presumption has or has not been rebutted, or that any statutory exception applies to any specific transfer involving Jordan Lee.

THE CORE PRESUMPTION AND WHAT "AFFECTING THE BURDEN OF PROOF" MEANS
Probate Code section 21380(a) provides that a provision of an instrument making a donative transfer to any of several specified categories of persons is presumed to be the product of fraud or undue influence. Section 21380(b) identifies exactly what kind of presumption this is and how it operates: it is "a presumption affecting the burden of proof," and it "may be rebutted by proving, by clear and convincing evidence, that the donative transfer was not the product of fraud or undue influence." So where this presumption applies and is rebuttable, it is not enough for the party defending the transfer to show, by an ordinary preponderance of the evidence, that fraud or undue influence did not produce it — the statute itself sets a higher, clear-and-convincing standard for that showing. California's general Evidence Code provision on this category of presumption, section 606, states what a "presumption affecting the burden of proof" does as a general matter across California law, independent of section 21380 itself: it "impose[s] upon the party against whom it operates the burden of proof as to the nonexistence of the presumed fact" — here, the burden of proving that the transfer was not the product of fraud or undue influence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) A provision of an instrument making a donative transfer to any of the following persons is presumed to be the product of fraud or undue influence:"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21380(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21380(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21380.)
  "(b) The presumption created by this section is a presumption affecting the burden of proof. The presumption may be rebutted by proving, by clear and convincing evidence, that the donative transfer was not the product of fraud or undue influence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21380(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21380(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21380.)
  "The effect of a presumption affecting the burden of proof is to impose upon the party against whom it operates the burden of proof as to the nonexistence of the presumed fact."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 606 (California Legislative Information text), Evid. C. § 606 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=606.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of the specific presumption Probate Code section 21380 creates and of the generic legal meaning of "presumption affecting the burden of proof" under Evidence Code section 606 — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instrument or transfer. Two sources are cited: Probate Code section 21380(a)-(b) (two subsections of one section, treated as one source) and Evidence Code section 606 (an independent source, cited because section 21380 itself invokes that term of art without redefining it). This clause does not itself list the categories of "disqualified person" the presumption reaches (a separate clause in this document covers that), does not cover the narrower circumstance in which section 21380 makes the presumption conclusive rather than rebuttable (also covered separately), and does not itself determine that any specific transfer is, or is not, subject to the presumption, or that any specific defense has, or has not, met the clear-and-convincing standard.

THE STATUTORY CATEGORIES OF "DISQUALIFIED PERSON"
Probate Code section 21380(a) attaches the presumption described in the preceding clause only where a donative transfer runs to one of seven specified categories of persons: (1) the person who drafted the instrument; (2) a person who transcribed the instrument, or caused it to be transcribed, and who was in a fiduciary relationship with the transferor when it was transcribed; (3) a care custodian of a transferor who is a dependent adult, but only if the instrument was executed during the period the care custodian provided services to the transferor, or within 90 days before or after that period; (4) a care custodian who married, or began cohabiting or a domestic partnership with, a dependent-adult transferor while providing services, or within 90 days after those services were last provided, if the transfer occurred or the instrument was executed less than six months after that marriage, cohabitation, or partnership began; (5) a person related by blood or affinity, within the third degree, to a person described in categories (1) through (3); (6) a cohabitant or employee of a person described in categories (1) through (3); and (7) a partner, shareholder, or employee of a law firm in which a person described in category (1) or (2) holds an ownership interest. The terms "care custodian" and "dependent adult," used in categories (3) and (4), carry the specific statutory definitions given in Probate Code sections 21362 and 21366 within this same statutory part, rather than their everyday meanings.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) A provision of an instrument making a donative transfer to any of the following persons is presumed to be the product of fraud or undue influence: (1) The person who drafted the instrument. (2) A person who transcribed the instrument or caused it to be transcribed and who was in a fiduciary relationship with the transferor when the instrument was transcribed. (3) A care custodian of a transferor who is a dependent adult, but only if the instrument was executed during the period in which the care custodian provided services to the transferor, or within 90 days before or after that period. (4) A care custodian who commenced a marriage, cohabitation, or domestic partnership with a transferor who is a dependent adult while providing services to that dependent adult, or within 90 days after those services were last provided to the dependent adult, if the donative transfer occurred, or the instrument was executed, less than six months after the marriage, cohabitation, or domestic partnership commenced. (5) A person who is related by blood or affinity, within the third degree, to any person described in paragraphs (1) to (3), inclusive. (6) A cohabitant or employee of any person described in paragraphs (1) to (3), inclusive. (7) A partner, shareholder, or employee of a law firm in which a person described in paragraph (1) or (2) has an ownership interest."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21380(a)(1)-(7) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21380(a)(1)-(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21380.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the seven specific categories that trigger the section 21380 presumption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, and not a claim that any specific person actually falls into any of these categories on any specific facts. This clause quotes a single statutory subsection, (a), with its seven paragraphs; they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. The "care custodian" and "dependent adult" definitions (Probate Code §§ 21362 and 21366) are not requoted in this clause: this corpus already independently verifies and quotes both definitions in full, word-for-word identical to the text refetched for this project, in the existing Omitted Spouse and Omitted Child (Pretermitted Heir) Information Sheet's clause on the omitted-spouse care-custodian exception — this clause cross-references rather than duplicates that verified text. This clause does not cover the narrower rule making the presumption conclusive, rather than rebuttable, for certain of these categories, which a separate clause in this document addresses.

WHEN THE PRESUMPTION CANNOT BE REBUTTED, AND WHO PAYS IF REBUTTAL FAILS
Probate Code section 21380(c) narrows the ordinary rebuttable rule stated in subdivision (b) for a specific subset of transfers: "Notwithstanding subdivision (b), with respect to a donative transfer to the person who drafted the donative instrument, or to a person who is related to, or associated with, the drafter as described in paragraph (5), (6), or (7) of subdivision (a), the presumption created by this section is conclusive." By its own terms, this conclusive-presumption rule reaches only a transfer to the drafter personally, or to a blood or affinity relative, cohabitant, employee, or law-firm partner, shareholder, or employee of the drafter as described in paragraphs (5) through (7) of subdivision (a) — a transfer to a fiduciary who merely transcribed the instrument, or to a care custodian described in paragraph (3) or (4), remains subject only to the ordinary rebuttable presumption described in an earlier clause of this document, not this conclusive one. Separately, section 21380(d) attaches a cost-shifting consequence where a rebuttal is attempted and fails: "If a beneficiary is unsuccessful in rebutting the presumption, the beneficiary shall bear all costs of the proceeding, including reasonable attorney's fees."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) Notwithstanding subdivision (b), with respect to a donative transfer to the person who drafted the donative instrument, or to a person who is related to, or associated with, the drafter as described in paragraph (5), (6), or (7) of subdivision (a), the presumption created by this section is conclusive."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21380(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21380(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21380.)
  "(d) If a beneficiary is unsuccessful in rebutting the presumption, the beneficiary shall bear all costs of the proceeding, including reasonable attorney’s fees."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21380(d) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21380(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21380.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific, narrower set of transfers to which section 21380 attaches a conclusive rather than rebuttable presumption, and of the cost-shifting consequence that attaches when a rebuttal attempt fails — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer. Both subdivisions (c) and (d) are quoted from the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. The statute's own text does not address, and this clause does not resolve, whether subdivision (d)'s cost-shifting rule has any application to a transfer subject to subdivision (c)'s conclusive presumption, where no rebuttal attempt is legally possible in the first place; that is a gap in the statutory text itself, not a gap this clause fills. This clause does not itself determine that any specific transfer falls within the conclusive-presumption category, or that any specific rebuttal attempt has succeeded or failed.

STATUTORY EXCEPTIONS THAT REMOVE A TRANSFER FROM SECTION 21380 ENTIRELY
Probate Code section 21382 lists six categories of instruments or transfers to which the section 21380 presumption does not apply at all: (a) except as provided for the care-custodian-marriage category in section 21380(a)(4), a donative transfer to a person related by blood or affinity, within the fourth degree, to the transferor, or who is the transferor's cohabitant; (b) an instrument drafted or transcribed by such a fourth-degree relative or cohabitant; (c) an instrument approved under a specified court-order procedure, after full disclosure of the relationships of the persons involved; (d) a donative transfer to a federal, state, or local public entity, to an entity that qualifies for a federal tax exemption under Internal Revenue Code section 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(19), or to a trust holding transferred property for such an entity; (e) a donative transfer of property valued at $5,000 or less, where the transferor's total estate equals or exceeds the amount stated in a separate Probate Code section governing small estates; and (f) an instrument executed outside California by a transferor who was not a California resident when the instrument was executed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Section 21380 does not apply to any of the following instruments or transfers: (a) Except as provided in paragraph (4) of subdivision (a) of Section 21380, a donative transfer to a person who is related by blood or affinity, within the fourth degree, to the transferor or is the cohabitant of the transferor. (b) An instrument that is drafted or transcribed by a person who is related by blood or affinity, within the fourth degree, to the transferor or is the cohabitant of the transferor. (c) An instrument that is approved pursuant to an order under Article 10 (commencing with Section 2580) of Chapter 6 of Part 4 of Division 4, after full disclosure of the relationships of the persons involved. (d) A donative transfer to a federal, state, or local public entity, an entity that qualifies for an exemption from taxation under Section 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(19) of the Internal Revenue Code, or a trust holding the transferred property for the entity. (e) A donative transfer of property valued at five thousand dollars ($5,000) or less, if the total value of the transferor’s estate equals or exceeds the amount stated in Section 13100. (f) An instrument executed outside of California by a transferor who was not a resident of California when the instrument was executed."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21382 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21382 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21382.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific categories of instruments and transfers section 21382 places outside the reach of section 21380 entirely — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, and not a claim that any specific transfer actually qualifies for any of these six exceptions. This clause quotes the whole of a single statutory section, with its six lettered subdivisions, as one contiguous source rather than as independent corroborating sources. Note a scope point stated on the face of the statute itself, not this clause's own interpretation: the blood-or-affinity relationship that removes a transfer from section 21380 under subdivisions (a) and (b) here is measured within the fourth degree, a wider relationship than the third-degree relationship that can trigger the presumption in the first place under section 21380(a)(5) — the statute does not use the same degree of relationship on both sides of the presumption. This clause does not independently verify the cross-referenced court-order procedure in subdivision (c) or the small-estate dollar threshold cross-referenced in subdivision (e); it states only what section 21382 itself says about them.

A SEPARATE ROUTE AROUND THE PRESUMPTION: AN INDEPENDENT ATTORNEY'S CERTIFICATE OF REVIEW
Separate from the exceptions in section 21382, Probate Code section 21384 provides an additional route by which a donative transfer can fall outside the section 21380 presumption: the statute provides that a donative transfer "is not subject to Section 21380 if the instrument is reviewed by an independent attorney" who counsels the transferor, outside the presence of any heir or proposed beneficiary, about the nature and consequences of the intended transfer, attempts to determine whether it is the result of fraud or undue influence, and signs and delivers to the transferor a certificate in a specific form the statute itself sets out — a "Certificate of Independent Review." Section 21384 also restricts who may serve in that reviewing role: under section 21384(c), an attorney who drafted the instrument may review and certify that same instrument only where the disqualified person at issue is a care custodian; in every other circumstance, the statute states that the drafting attorney "may not review and certify the instrument."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) A donative transfer is not subject to Section 21380 if the instrument is reviewed by an independent attorney who counsels the transferor, out of the presence of any heir or proposed beneficiary, about the nature and consequences of the intended transfer, including the effect of the intended transfer on the transferor’s heirs and on any beneficiary of a prior donative instrument, attempts to determine if the intended transfer is the result of fraud or undue influence, and signs and delivers to the transferor an original certificate in substantially the following form:"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21384(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21384(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21384.)
  "(c) An attorney who drafts an instrument can review and certify the same instrument pursuant to this section, but only as to a donative transfer to a care custodian. In all other circumstances, an attorney who drafts an instrument may not review and certify the instrument."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21384(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 21384(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21384.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that this certificate-of-independent-review route exists and of its central operative requirement and drafting-attorney restriction — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, and not an exhaustive account of section 21384. Consistent with this research project's intended scope, this clause deliberately does not quote or independently verify the certificate's full required language (the balance of subdivision (a)), the cross-referenced definition of "independent attorney" in Probate Code section 21370, the client-representation limit in subdivision (b), or the delivery-to-the-drafting-attorney requirement in subdivision (d); none of that text is described or relied on here. The two subdivisions quoted, (a) and (c), are drawn from the same statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources. This clause does not itself determine that any specific attorney review or certificate meets section 21384's requirements for any specific instrument.

CERTIFICATION AND SIGNATURE
I certify that I have read this information sheet describing California's statutory presumption of fraud or undue influence affecting certain donative transfers to disqualified persons, Probate Code sections 21380 through 21392, and that it states generally applicable California law rather than a conclusion about whether any specific transfer, instrument, or person involving Jordan Lee is subject to, exempt from, or has satisfied, that presumption.

Executed on September 4, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Pat Morgan: _________________________

Printed name: _________________________

Section 21384 also restricts who may serve in that reviewing role: under section 21384(c), an attorney who drafted the instrument may review and certify that same instrument only where the disqualified person at issue is a care custodian; in every other circumstance, the statute states that the drafting attorney "may not review and certify the instrument."
